Importantly, we exited the year with a great deal of momentum. In the fourth quarter, we delivered 9% adjusted EBITDA growth and 20% adjusted EPS growth. Turning to our segment performance. In the Americas, design NSR increased 6% this quarter.

The adjusted operating margin was 20.6%, up 20 basis points from the prior year. n the fourth quarter, backlog in the design business was up high single digits as well as up sequentially while the pipeline growing even faster. This positions us well for continued growth in fiscal 2027 and beyond. Turning to the International segment. NSR growth accelerated again this quarter, up 5%, led by ongoing strength in the U.K. and Australia. The adjusted operating margin was 14.8%, which set a new quarterly record and was up 270 basis points. This performance reflects growth in our higher-margin markets, improved utilization and initial returns on our strategic investments.

Our International backlog growth also continues to be strong with several large wins this year, including a significant metro rail project in Ireland during the fourth quarter. Turning to cash flow and capital allocation. We exceeded our prior free cash flow guidance for the year, reflecting underlying business performance. When combined with our strong balance sheet position with net leverage of 1.3x, we are able to continue to operate with certainty. As Troy noted, we increased our quarterly dividend by 10%, and we remain committed to double-digit annual growth in per share value of our dividend for the long term.

For your modeling, there is no workday impact for the full year. We expect segment adjusted operating margin and adjusted EBITDA margin expansion to 17.6%.

Our margins are benefiting from our overall growth mix shift from growing our higher-margin advisory business and benefits from our restructuring and technology investments. As always, this does not include any potential benefits from capital allocation actions not yet taken. Our tax rate is expected to be approximately 22%, and, consistent with prior years, we expect a lower rate in the first quarter. Gaurav Kapoor: Yes. I'll take that question. Right now, it is in the phase of what we call more agency work before the meat of our scope is delivered, that those large projects are going to kickstart in the second half of the year. And we also have -- even though for the year, there's no workday impact, just in the first quarter, we do have about half a day of impact as well. So when you look at the overall business, the design business, given the backlog growth, the CM business as well, that significant backlog growth in the first half, design business and second half is going to consistently going to deliver, but it will be tempered overall growth because of the CM business.

So there will be a ramp. I would say we're probably going to be at the low end of the range, maybe a little bit below low end of the range in the first quarter, and it will ramp up from there. And from a margin standpoint, I would say the delivery and the phasing is going to be very consistent to what you guys have seen last few years, including FY '26.

Between the first quarter and the second quarter, there generally is about 170 to 200 bps of differential, just given the number of workdays hours that are available. Therefore, our overhead cost and period costs are absorbed at a better clip in Q4 compared to Q1, and that consistently ramps up as well.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Adam Bubes with Goldman Sachs.

And the third part outside of the AI, which we've already spoken about, is continued focus on our EC delivery centers. Adam Bubes: And then on AI, can you just update us on the rollout of AI tools across the portfolio, which workflows are being impacted today? Any way to sort of quantify the early efficiency gains? But as we followed our development road map, as the development has become more robust and started to impact what we can actually deliver for our customers, it's not that we're focused on margin efficiencies or efficiencies. And so think about that as actually dramatically improving the outcomes or the returns on their infrastructure assets because of the way we're able to take technology and effectively partner with our teams of engineers working on those projects.

And so that -- I mean, you can think about that as having an impact on margins, but we think of that actually at this point is starting to have an impact on our ability to win, to win relationships, win projects and actually through those new relationships, actually win work that we hadn't done before even outside of engineering and design. So again, we're a year into this process. We're kind of working through our thoughtful road map of development and deployment. W. Rudd: Yes. Andy, I'll sort of confirm a few points that you already made for us. First of all is we are winning work that is longer in duration, so larger projects. And they're not directly linked to make sure that there is significant NSR growth to drive that margin expansion. So we have -- there's a lot of different blocks we have put in place, and that's why I say we have a lot of confidence and why we've delivered for the last 6 years, industry-leading margins.

Sangita Jain: Understood. And then is there any update that you can provide on the dispute resolution for the challenged Construction Management projects that you're pursuing? And any kind of updated time line on when we may hear more on those?

#3081. ‘We need more reviewers’: Finding Linux bugs is easy now – fixing them is another story

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Some Linux maintainers are quitting under the crushing strain of AI bug reports, while others see signs for hope.

Recently, Microsoft’s FORGE Lab reported that its AI scanning system, MDASH, turned up 59 upstream Linux kernel bug reports, including one flaw at least 21 years old. That’s less impressive than it sounds. For 2026, through Nov. 2, the Linux Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) team reported an average of 27 CVEs a day.

Why so many? Easy: in Linux, any bug can be a security bug. As Linux Torvalds told me in 2024, “Bugs will happen, and anything can be a security bug if somebody is clever enough to just figure out how to abuse it.” Besides, since Linux runs everything from smartphones to refrigerators to supercomputers, what may be a serious bug in one device may not even appear at all on another.

It’s not just Linux, though. In the latest Windows Patch Tuesday security release, Microsoft reported 726 CVEs. The vast majority of these bug reports are coming from AI programmers. Finding bugs on anything is no longer the hard part. But reviewing and fixing them is, and both Microsoft developers and kernel maintainers are struggling to keep up.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

As the FORGE Lab said, “Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance.” Turning its findings into reports took more than four person-months because “human effort [is] the bottleneck.”

That’s hurting the overworked maintainers. On Nov. 10, an ARM engineer and Linux kernel maintainer Lorenzo Stoakes gave up reviewing code. He’d been a reviewer for the memory-management core, misc, reclaim, and Rust-related sections. Stoakes, a kernel contributor since 2014,  wrote, “Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain.”

Stoakes added, “Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse. At first it was once in a while that I’d see slop. Then it was at least once a week. Then every few days. Nowadays it’s pretty much half of what I see, if not more.”

Also: Filing bugs for open-source apps is a huge help for devs – and easier than you think

He’s not alone. As Greg Kroah-Hartman, the Linux kernel stable maintainer, said in a Q&A session at Open Source Summit Europe, “We don’t have enough people to review them, the onslaught of the LLM-generated patches. We need more reviewers. We don’t have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years.”

It’s not all doom and gloom, though. Linux Torvalds, Linux’s creator, said in a recent Linux Kernel Mailing List (LKML) message that much of the new code in the Linux 7.4 rc 2 “was driven by various AI fixes.”

He continued, “that on the bpf [Berkeley Packet Filter]- side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true. I think most other areas haven’t reached that point yet, but it’s at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn. Don’t hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we’ll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.”

We can but hope. In an interview, Kroah-Hartman isn’t so optimistic. “We are getting closer, yes, but not quite there yet.”  He’s not even willing to give a guesstimate of when human-approved AI fixes will catch up with and overcome AI bug reports.

Also: I locked down my OpenClaw agent with Claude Code – then dared it to escape

Daniel Steinberg, the creator of the open-source cURL project, is also cautiously optimistic. Steinberg, who’s been especially critical of AI slop bug reports, told me in an interview that he now believes “we manage the flood pretty well so far, even if it goes a little up and down in periods depending exactly on who sends us a new set of findings this particular week.”

Still, while AI bugs remain a major headache for now, AI bug fixes, along with the work of thousands of maintainers, may finally be starting to stem the AI bug flood. I still foresee long days and nights of work ahead.

I also expect we’ll see more serious security breaches. In November alone, we saw a serious Linux TCP networking security hole revealed; the nasty Alpine Linux OpenSSH flaw; Alpine’s GitLab near-miss; and the wide-open PHP2Shell security problem, which many groups still haven’t patched.

#3080. VSCO launches its first native Mac photo editor with RAW support, batch editing, more

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

#3079. Five iOS 27 Toggles That Make Your iPhone Easier to Read and More Private

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

Whether it’s a new iPhone or an updated one, these five iOS 27 settings are worth checking before you settle in.

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo ship with iOS 27’s default settings, and so does any older iPhone that updated this fall. Those defaults include a strong Liquid Glass effect, automatic subtitles on videos and a Siri that saves and syncs your conversations.

They’re easy to change once you know where to look. Here are five settings worth adjusting, whether you’re setting up a new phone or finally getting around to it on your current one.

Read more: Win a New Apple Watch in CNET Big Guessing Game Contest

Apple introduced Liquid Glass with iOS 26, giving menus, buttons, notifications and other interface elements a translucent appearance. Not everyone was a fan of the new design, and with iOS 27, you now get more control over exactly how transparent the interface looks.

Go to Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass. Drag the slider to the right to add more tint and opacity, making buttons and text easier to distinguish from whatever is behind them. Moving it left makes the interface more transparent.

If the most opaque setting still isn’t enough, go to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and turn on Reduce Transparency. This makes translucent backgrounds more solid across iOS, although it overrides the regular Liquid Glass appearance controls.

More tint makes Liquid Glass easier to read.

The new Siri AI works similarly t ChatGPT or Claude in iOS 27. It now comes complete with a dedicated app where you can revisit previous conversations. Those chats sync through iCloud so you can start a conversation on your iPhone and continue it on another Apple device, such as your Mac.

By default, iOS 27 keeps those conversations forever, but there is a way to automatically get rid of older conversations if you don’t want them piling up.

If you don’t need a permanent archive of everything you ask Siri, go to Settings > Siri > Keep Conversations and choose 30 Days or 1 Year. Selecting either option permanently deletes conversations beyond that timeframe.

Siri keeps your conversations forever unless you choose a shorter limit.

While you’re there, tap Opens To and select A New Conversation if you want the Siri app to open with a blank chat instead of showing your recent conversations every time.

Siri AI requires an iPhone 15 Pro or 15 Pro Max, iPhone Air or an iPhone 16 or later.

iOS 27 puts a new Write with Siri button above the keyboard in apps including Messages, Mail and Notes. You can ask Siri AI to draft something from scratch, proofread what you’ve written or rewrite it in a different tone.

The thing is, I’m not a big fan of the AI writing tools, so I don’t use them at all.

Screen Time lets you completely disable Siri’s writing tools.

This disables access to the writing tools across your iPhone, rather than simply hiding the keyboard button, so only do this if you don’t use Apple’s AI writing tools at all. You can return to the same menu and choose Allow if you want them back. Apple documents the restriction under its Apple Intelligence Screen Time controls.

Introduced back in iOS 17, Siri can now wake up when you simply say “Siri” instead of “Hey Siri.” The one-word command is convenient, but it also makes accidental activations more likely whenever someone says Siri’s name in a conversation or a video they’re watching online.

Siri goes absolutely bonkers whenever I’m in work meetings about Apple features.

To disable the feature, go to Settings > Siri > Talk to Siri. Choose “Hey Siri” instead of “Siri.”

Requiring “Hey Siri” can help prevent accidental activations.

You’ll still be able to bring up Siri with your voice, but the extra word makes it less likely to wake up when you aren’t talking to it directly.

This isn’t exclusive to iOS 27, but it’s been annoying me more recently, so thought I would throw it in here, especially with Siri AI being the prominent feature on this update.

iOS 27 now automatically shows subtitles on videos in Photos, Safari and other apps that use Apple’s video player. I don’t mind captions when I need them, but they can take up too much of the video and distract me from whatever I’m watching.

They don’t appear randomly though. By default, iOS can turn them on when the video is in another language, when your iPhone is muted or when you skip back.

Whenever subtitles appear in Apple’s video player, you can tap the video to show the playback controls, tap the More Controls button, select Subtitles and choose Off.

If iOS keeps turning them on because it thinks the video is in another language, go to Settings > Accessibility > Subtitles & Captioning. Under Automatic Subtitles, turn off When Languages Don’t Match.

The same menu also has switches for Show When Muted and Show on Skip Back, so you can disable those behaviors individually without turning off every automatic subtitle feature.

You can also disable each automatic subtitle trigger individually.

Some apps and websites use their own video players, so you may need to find a separate CC or subtitles button instead.

#3078. I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A new option called Memory summary lets you see and control the things that Gemini AI knows about you.

Like any AI, Google Gemini wants to remember things about you. The purported reason is to help tailor and personalize your conversations. But remember that your personal details may also wind up training the AI or even being reviewed by actual humans. With that in mind, you might want to find out just what Gemini knows about you. And now you can.

Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work

With a new option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time. These may be tidbits from your conversations or things that you directly told the AI. Even better, you can add or remove any details just by editing the memory or issuing your request directly to Gemini.

This new capability is available in Gemini across the board, so you can access it at the Gemini website, in the mobile iOS and Android apps, and in the Windows and Mac desktop apps.

Launch Gemini via the web or in one of the mobile or desktop apps. In the left pane displaying your previous chats, select the Settings icon at the bottom. At the Settings screen, select Personal Intelligence and then click or tap Memory summary. If the option is grayed out, it means the Memory feature is turned off. To proceed, turn it back on. You can always turn if off again afterward if you wish.

You’ll then see the individual details by category. My summary arranged the information across such categories as Essentials, Business & Career, Reading & Interests, and Culinary Preferences. Go down the list to see the individual items in each category. To view a recent history, tap the three dot-icon at the top and select Memory history. This shows you the latest changes and updates to Gemini’s memory.

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

What if Gemini’s memory includes details that are too personal or just incorrect? No problem. You can alter the AI’s memories of you. At the website or in one of the desktop apps, click the pencil icon at the top. Now you’re able to directly edit the text to add, remove, or revise specific details. After you’ve made your changes, just click Save.

For example, my summary said that I lived in Madison County. I have no idea where Gemini got that notion, as I live in New York. Here, I revised the text and saved the changes, which then synced across the Gemini website and apps.

The mobile apps have no direct editing capability. But there’s another method that works both on mobile and on the desktop. Just tell Gemini what change you want to make. At the prompt, type and speak your request, and the AI will carry it out for you.

As an example, my summary said that I run a business called Batter Up selling collectible baseball cards. That’s not at all true. I had once referred to such a store only to test Gemini’s image creation skills to design a logo for a baseball card seller. Here, I simply told Gemini that I don’t run a business called Batter Up and asked it to remove that item from its memory. Poof, that detail quickly disappeared.

Galaxy Claw could make calls and send text messages for you.

Samsung is expected to unveil its Galaxy S27 lineup early next year, and a personal AI assistant might be arriving as well. The so-called Galaxy Claw could perform a variety of functions, including making phone calls, sending text messages and creating appointments, according to Android Authority.

The tech news website discovered Galaxy Claw while digging into Samsung’s Personal Agent Core app, which is a new AI system that connects AI across Samsung apps and Google services. This new system can also pull data from your calendar, Gmail, text messages, delivery info and other sources and also autonomously perform tasks upon your instructions.

Android Authority said that coding details for the Personal Agent Core app were shared by The Cipher Project, a Telegram channel that often leaks Samsung software updates, One UI features and unreleased device functions.

A representative for Samsung did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Samsung has had AI functionality on its phones and other devices since January 2024, when the company introduced Galaxy AI. The main capabilities at that launch included Circle to Search — allowing users to search for anything on the screen — as well as live language translation and photo editing.

Over the past two-plus years, Samsung has integrated more AI functionality into its devices, including Google Gemini and Gemini Live. Although Samsung devices have plenty of AI to do things for you, it primarily operates on your command rather than acting as an autonomous agent.

The new Galaxy Claw system might launch at Samsung Unpacked in January or February, when Samsung could release the Galaxy S27 series, which could include the Ultra flagship. Samsung has not officially announced what products it will launch at Unpacked.

According to Android Authority, the Galaxy Claw could connect to various apps on your phone and perform functions for you. Those apps could include Calendar, Contacts, Gallery, Gmail, Messages, Notifications, Perplexity, Phone and Voice Recorder.

So, in essence, the Claw could create appointments, write and send emails and make phone calls. For example, you could have Claw set up a meeting and send calendar notifications to the attendees with an attached agenda. Or perhaps Claw could call someone for you to tell them where you’re going.

Android Authority said other components could be included — Daily Brief, Device Cleaner, Travel Planner and a dedicated widget.

Those tasks would be a major step up from what Galaxy AI can currently do on Samsung phones — live translation, text drafting, photo editing, scam call detection and more.

Adding agentic AI won’t justify the $1,400 or even $1,500 price tag for the S27 Ultra but could help generate customer loyalty, says tech reviewer Jon Rettinger.

“People buy the Ultra for the camera, the screen and the S Pen, and that won’t change next year,” Rettinger told CNET. “Where an agent could matter is keeping people. If Galaxy Claw is reading my Gmail, my calendar and my texts and quietly handling the busywork, switching phones gets a lot harder, because I’d be walking away from an assistant that knows how my week runs.”

Rettinger said Samsung would be wise to include the Galaxy Claw with the new devices and not as a separate subscription service.

“So, now the pitch is $1,500 for the phone, then a monthly fee for the feature that’s supposed to justify the phone,” Rettinger said. “That’s a tough sell. If Samsung wants this to move hardware, it should come included on the Ultra.”

People apparently will maintain authority and control over Galaxy Claw, according to Android Authority. The new system would request access to sensitive data such as contacts, photos and calendar events, as well as permission to execute functions such as sending text messages and making calls. The Claw wouldn’t go rogue on you, in other words.

Samsung users might also be able to schedule the Claw to do tasks and functions regularly. Perhaps you need to email or text weekly reminders to someone about something. You could instruct the AI on the task and when to do it each week. It might only require a simple prompt from you, such as, “Please remind my son to take out the garbage by 8 a.m. Monday mornings.”

Android Authority said tasks could be scheduled by hour, day, weekly and custom intervals. Users would also be able to cancel or modify scheduled tasks and check task history.

#3074. AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Rapidly advancing AI models are making it cheaper and easier to uncover critical vulnerabilities, but it's a double-edged sword - and a gift to hackers.

The best AI models on the market couldn’t find zero-days earlier this year, but now they can in less than 15 minutes and at a cost of a few bucks, according to a new report from penetration testing firm Xint.io. The findings raise questions about how vulnerabilities will be discovered and exploited in the future.

Every major AI developer is working at breakneck speed to improve model effectiveness. At the same time, token prices continue to fall, with studies showing that the average cost of tokens, which varies by domain, has dropped by about 47% per quarter since 2023 and 15% last month alone, due to intense competition among companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

This is good news for businesses trying to harness AI for productivity and new services, but as token prices fall, it has also become cheaper for attackers to launch AI-assisted attacks, including software breaches caused by exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

A report published by Xint.io examines how popular AI models have evolved over the past year to the point where cybersecurity tasks that would have failed only months ago now succeed. The team analyzed seven models launched since February 2026: two from OpenAI, three from Anthropic, and two open-source models from DeepSeek and Z.ai. The team tracked, over time, how they performed in finding a target vulnerability.

The target of this research was a security flaw in Google’s V8 engine. Tracked as CVE-2026-102321, the type confusion bug leading to remote code execution (RCE) was disclosed to the Google Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) by Xint researcher Taisic Yun and so was not present in the AI models’ training datasets.

The research scope was limited to a set of source files, including the file containing the vulnerability, and each model was instructed to search for security issues within these files.

Xint’s first test was conducted in February. After 25 hours and $350 of scanning, the best models then available still couldn’t find the critical vulnerability.

In July, GPT 5.6 Sol found the zero-day flaw for $22 in 44 minutes.

Also: Finding Linux bugs is easy – fixing them is another story

By September, GPT 6 Sol discovered the bug in 13 minutes for only $4.24 with its first guided prompt.

Only three of the seven models found the bug: GPT 6 Sol, GPT 5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5, all launched from July onward. GPT 5.6 Sol needed two prompts, while Claude Opus 5 found it on its first try but at a higher cost of $43.40.

DeepSeek’s and Z.ai’s models failed the task.

The researchers say that the combination of AI model development and low token prices means that “mediocre hackers” can now use frontier models effectively to discover and potentially exploit vulnerabilities, and “while we are still far from complete amateurs using unharnessed models to hack systems and applications, what used to be considered too hard and costly to be worth the effort of the average hacker is now reachable.”

As a result, organizations need to adjust their security posture accordingly — but falling token costs and evolving AI skills and speed can also work in your favor.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac

There’s nothing stopping an organization’s security team or pentesters from running the same checks themselves to find vulnerabilities before threat actors do. AI-assisted tests, arguably, are no longer something that can be pushed back to next year’s budgetary review. By performing a risk assessment that focuses on likely weak spots, such as public-facing services or a digital supply chain that hasn’t been audited for years, organizations can mitigate the risk AI-enabled cyberattacks pose.

Zero-day vulnerabilities are unknown to vendors, and a patch might not be available when they go public or are actively exploited in the wild. So, AI can only go so far, but it can free up your defenders for tasks that need the human touch. Furthermore, maintaining zero-trust access controls, segmenting and shoring up your network’s defenses, and monitoring endpoints for signs of suspicious behavior can do as much as, or more than, AI.

As Xint notes, “expertise still matters” when it comes to instructing AI models to discover vulnerabilities. In some cases, the models couldn’t find the target vulnerability without guidance, so additional runs were needed, increasing time and cost.

“Software breaches still require some level of technical proficiency,” the researchers say, “but no longer top-of-the-distribution expertise.”

It targets premium buyers across 24 countries, emphasizing a user enterprise model that integrates lifestyle services with vehicle ownership. No single customer accounts for more than 10% of its revenue, providing a diversified sales base.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $13.1 billion, an increase of approximately 33.1% from the prior year. Despite this growth, the company reported a net loss of about $2.2 billion for the period. While the net margin improved from the previous two years, it remained negative at roughly 17.1%. (Note that figures have been converted from Chinese Yuan as of the publication date).

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 6.3x, which measures total debt against the value of shareholder equity. The current ratio, which gauges the ability to cover short-term obligations with current assets, is roughly 1.0x. Free cash flow, or cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was negative $461.2 million. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 59.8% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Tesla operates as a vertically integrated manufacturer of electric vehicles and energy storage systems, selling directly to consumers without a traditional dealership network. It serves a diverse group of residential and utility-scale customers, while partnering with firms like Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CYATY +0.35%) for battery cells. This strategy allows the company to capture value across the entire energy ecosystem.

For FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $94.8 billion, a decrease of nearly 2.9% year over year. The company recorded net income of roughly $3.8 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 4%. This represents a decline from the double-digit net margins seen in previous fiscal years.

As of the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1x, indicating a very low level of debt relative to equity. The current ratio is roughly 2.2x, suggesting a strong ability to meet immediate financial commitments. Tesla generated significant free cash flow of nearly $6.2 billion, providing ample capital for reinvestment.

NIO faces challenges related to its capital-intensive battery-swapping network and its expansion into highly competitive international markets. The company must manage heavy research and development costs while striving for profitability among consumer discretionary stocks facing fluctuating demand. Geopolitical tensions and trade barriers in Europe and North America also pose significant hurdles for its global growth ambitions.

Tesla encounters risks involving the complex production ramp-up of new products like the Cybercab and Optimus robot. It is also heavily dependent on the continued advancement of autonomous driving software and the time and attention of its chief executive. Intense competition from global manufacturers and sensitivity to macroeconomic factors, such as interest rates, can further affect vehicle demand and pricing.

NIO currently trades at a significantly lower sales multiple than Tesla, although Tesla remains the only profitable company between the two based on recent earnings.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

The P/S ratio measures a company's market price against its sales over the past twelve months. Meanwhile, the Forward P/E compares the share price to future earnings estimates.

For investors seeking EV automaker stocks, NIO and Tesla offer two strong brands in two significant global car markets.

Looking at NIO, the EV market in mainland China is booming: fully two-thirds of all vehicles sold in the country these days are classified as EVs or plug-in hybrids (PHEVs). Still, new car sales in China plunged about 20% in the first half of 2026 compared to the first half of 2025, even as EVs and PHEVs continued to gain market share. The central government halved its credit for buying EVs this year too, which should be impacting demand, although in the current five-year plan, the Communist government has EVs as a core part of its central economic plan.

NIO management is saying it will be able to post 8% sales growth for the third quarter of the current fiscal year, but August deliveries of almost 36,000 units were about 10% of the run rate needed to hit that mark, according to a report from CFRA. Wall Street sees NIO tallying sales of $19.2 billion in 2026, growth of more than 46%. It should come with a much narrower net loss of $300 million, according to consensus estimates.

Tesla, meanwhile, faces a muddled outlook in the U.S. The Big Beautiful Bill removed incentives for buying EVs in the U.S., an obvious negative for Tesla. Third-quarter EV sales were down sharply from 2025, although that quarter is believed to have pulled forward consumer demand for EVs ahead of the expiration of the GOP's signature bill in recent years. Yet in October, EV sales posted their first rise over 2025, as elevated gas prices from the Iran war sent shoppers seeking alternatives to fossil fuel vehicles. On the other hand, Tesla is killing off the Cybertruck, a massive failure on the scale of the famous Edsel from Ford Motor Co. (F -1.99%) in the late 1950s.

Wall Street has also long been expecting that Elon Musk will seek to combine Tesla with Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +3.16%), which has brought a type of arbitrage to the shares.

So which is the better buy? Leave the inside baseball of a potential SpaceX merger to the pros. NIO is the simpler story here and the far better-valued automaker, even as it operates in a fiercely competitive Chinese market and does not come cheap in its own right, valuation-wise.

#3071. A New Study Finds Hyperscale Data Centers Emit as Much Carbon as Denmark

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Harvard researchers collected metrics on more than 400 data centers to determine their energy use and carbon emissions.

During the midterm elections, Americans made one thing very clear: Data centers must be reined in.

A vast majority of communities across the country voted to ban or restrict the construction of data centers, as concerns about their impact on the environment and public health grow.

A new study by Harvard researchers shows that these fears are not unfounded. The findings published today in Nature Sustainability show that the carbon emissions and energy use of hyperscale data centers amount to as much as those of entire states and more than those of the country of Denmark.

I spoke with Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics and lead author of the paper, to discuss how the team collected data on energy use despite a lack of industry transparency, the rapid evolution of AI infrastructure and future research goals.

Hyperscale data centers are the largest and most powerful data center facilities, featuring thousands of servers to power cloud computing, model training and the global use of AI. Guidi said he was inspired to look into data center emissions and the broader impacts of generative AI after reading a paper on bitcoin mining’s electricity use, which found that just 34 mining facilities, combined, consumed as much electricity as the entire city of Los Angeles.

The study narrowed in on 403 of these facilities to provide the most up-to-date and transparent measures of their electricity use and carbon emissions between May 2024 and April 2025.

Tech companies are not quick to disclose their energy use, so Guidi and his team had to circumvent these obstacles to get accurate metrics. The team used satellite imagery to narrow down 675 candidate sites to 403 verified facilities, estimated annual electricity consumption, and linked them to Environmental Protection Agency data to measure each facility’s carbon emissions.

“I would say the data preparation, data collection and validation were 100% the toughest part of the whole project,” Guidi said during a phone interview, explaining that there is a need for transparency and people should have access to this data.

During the study, the team found that these hyperscale data centers emitted 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, more than the entire country of Denmark and far exceeding the last peer-reviewed estimate from 2018. The 403 facilities also used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity during the testing period — about 1.8% of all US electricity consumption.

A majority of the electricity (54%) that powers these hyperscale data centers comes from natural gas and coal, despite many tech companies signing corporate pledges to make substantial investments in renewable energy. Fossil fuels have long been known to generate massive amounts of carbon dioxide, exacerbating global warming and climate change, despite many of these tech companies. “We need to distinguish between what companies commit to on paper, and then the actual physical emissions associated with the whole powering of these infrastructures,” Guidi said.

The Harvard team also pointed out that the paper’s data is from last spring, meaning the industry’s 2026 footprint is certainly substantially larger today.

“I feel like the pace at which the industry is growing is really outpacing the pace at which people like us — scientists — are working in order to understand (HDC) impacts,” Guidi said. “And we’re lagging behind because of the way the system is made.”

As data centers scale and expand, the research will need to as well, the researchers said. The team is already working to expand its dataset to investigate the broader public health consequences of hyperscale data centers, including water consumption and noise pollution.

#3070. Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Underground brokers are selling access to hijacked enterprise AI accounts, with companies footing the usage bill, Google reports.

In just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming. Bad actors steal credentials for those models through LLMjacking — and the marketplace is evolving.

Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.

Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors

Organizations have poured billions of dollars into AI development and deployment, although the amount they spend on AI tokens every month varies. According to Ramp AI index data, among firms paying for AI, the top 1% spent over $10,000 per employee per month, compared with around $16 for the median firm. When employees have access to AI models, companies may introduce spending caps, but smaller outfits may overlook them.

LLMjacking is the theft of AI-related credentials, including usernames and passwords, or API keys, used to access AI models. This gives cybercriminals the opportunity to use tokens and AI resources belonging to a victim organization (or individual), typically with usage-based billing or subscriptions with no fixed cap.

With these credentials, an unauthorized user could run high-resource computing tasks, manage their own malicious AI deployments, extract and steal corporate data from the AI’s memory, or even poison training data. To add insult to injury, if demand outstrips the limits of the victim’s subscription, cybercriminals can rack up high usage costs that the victim is then on the hook for.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

John Hultquist, chief analyst for GTIG, previously said the cybersecurity unit has seen a “major increase” in LLMjacking over 2026, so we can assume this trend will likely continue into 2027 and beyond.

AI access is now a lucrative illegal business in its own right, leading to what Google calls LLM Mixers: “illicit storefronts” that provide unauthorized access to AI services and underlying proxy infrastructure.

After analyzing LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language marketplaces, GTIG researchers found that most offer access not only to frontier models from AI labs, but also to jailbroken models marketed as suitable for malicious purposes.

However, it doesn’t seem that many of these cybercriminal groups can agree on “reasonable” pricing, with prices swinging wildly depending on the models offered and the credentials available.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard

Free trial credentials fetch far less than enterprise credentials, as you would expect. Token prices for business use ranged from $0.10 to $25, and one vendor, APIMart, increased its token price fivefold once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Other vendors offer subscription-based pricing.

This might not seem like much at the lower tiers, but Sysdig estimates LLMJacking could cost around $46,000 based on earlier models, and even over $100,000 per day on cutting-edge models. Mandiant research published earlier this month recorded incidents with illicit AI usage exceeding $100,000 in only 24 hours, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.

While direct credentials can be sold, the infrastructure element is also an interesting service offering. Google’s threat team said in the report that the sale of LLM infrastructure “routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”

LLM Mixers look similar to the rest of the cybercriminal underground economy, in which traders tend to specialize in one or two parts of an attack chain. For example, an LLM Mixer offers the access and infrastructure needed to exploit an enterprise AI model, while its partners might break into victim networks to secure initial access or buy stolen credentials from operators of infostealer malware.

Avoid LLMjacking and having your organization’s AI added to a Mixer’s menu similarly to how you would prevent intrusions into SaaS applications and cloud setups: managing access, monitoring, and imposing restrictions.

Usage and spending are the first areas to tackle. By setting limits on how many tokens can be issued and used across every AI service and account, and by alerting when usage suddenly spikes, organizations can limit damage if an account is compromised and stop massive bills before they rack up.

Organizations should also try to prevent their keys from ending up in the hands of cyberattackers in the first place. Google recommends using a secrets manager that securely stores and frequently rotates API keys, and running audits to detect quiet probing, misconfigurations, or shadow accounts.

It’s also advisable, across the board, to implement phishing protections and multi-factor authentication (MFA) to make the business of stealing credentials or compromising your accounts and networks more difficult in the first place.

#3069. The Google Wallet app is now available on iOS

Google Wallet is now available on iOS to “organize purchases, tickets, boarding passes, and more in one easy place” in the US.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:

App navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

The next tab shows a list of recent transactions associated with Google. The Wallet app will display purchase emails and summarize them. You also get a list of Passes, which you can pin/unpin from the homepage, and payment methods saved to your Google Account.

The ‘plus’ FAB (floating action button) lets you add loyalty, gift, and payment cards (for use in Chrome). There’s a convenient “Everything else” camera scanner that can be used to digitize anything else.

The other main reason Google Wallet now exists on iOS is that the company wants the app to be a “secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google.”

Record orders and a $2.7 billion backlog signal demand strength ahead.

Management reported that Powell (POWL -0.23%) achieved record financial results for the 2026 fiscal year, highlighted by record revenue, earnings, and cash flow. To support this growth, the company is significantly expanding its manufacturing footprint in Texas and Ohio, with additional capacity coming online through fiscal 2027. Management indicated that market demand remains active in the liquefied natural gas and electrical infrastructure segments, providing visibility for project deliveries into fiscal 2028.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Powell Industries Fiscal 2026 Fourth Quarter and Full Year Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note that this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Mr. Robert Winters of Alpha IR. Please go ahead, sir.

For more information, please refer to the company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. With that, I'll now turn the call over to Brett.

Brett Cope: Thank you, Bobby, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today to review Powell's fiscal 2026 fourth quarter and full year results. I will make a few comments and then turn the call over to Mike for more financial commentary before we take your questions. Before I turn to our results for the quarter and full year, I want to take a moment to recognize the passing of Tom Powell, our former Chairman and CEO, who passed away on September 23 at the age of 86. Tom first began working at Powell at just 14 years old, spending his summers on the manufacturing floor of the company his father founded.

Over the decades that followed, he helped shape Powell into the company it is today, building a culture of hard work, product excellence and a commitment to our customers that remains central to our success. When Tom announced his retirement from the Board, he expressed his belief that Powell's best years were still ahead. He was right, and I believe the progress we've made is a testament to the foundation he helped build. On behalf of the entire Powell team, I extend our deepest condolences to Tom's family and all those who knew him. With that, I'd like to turn to our financial results and the progress we've made over the past year.

Our fourth quarter capped what was truly a transformational year for Powell. We closed fiscal 2026 with record revenue, earnings and cash flow as well as record orders and a total backlog of $2.7 billion, the highest in our 79-year history. I want to start by thanking the entire Powell team. The level of collaboration we have seen across our divisions is outstanding and to our employees across all the geographies where we work and live, a job well done. This year has been outstanding, and our team members are the reason that we are able to say yes to the opportunities that our customers have and continue to bring an award to Powell.

Turning to our results for the quarter. Revenue grew 33% to $397 million compared to the fourth quarter of the prior year. Growth was once again led by strength in the oil and gas and commercial and other industrial end markets, complemented by solid contributions from the electric utility end market. Our continued focus on productivity and project execution delivered a gross margin of 34.9%, resulting in earnings of $2.23 per diluted share. We booked $710 million of new orders in the quarter, which was up 162% compared to the prior year and was the second highest order total in Powell's history, surpassed only by the record $934 million that we booked in the prior quarter.

Included in this quarter's total were 2 mega orders, LNG order at roughly $250 million and an order in the data center space valued at approximately $85 million. For the full year, revenue grew 14% to a record $1.3 billion and gross margins ended at 31.3%, resulting in earnings of $6.04 per diluted share. We booked $2.6 billion of new orders, more than double what we booked in fiscal 2025 for a full year book-to-bill of 2x. As a result, we ended the year with a backlog of $2.7 billion, up over $300 million sequentially and $1.3 billion higher than a year ago.

Our visibility now extends well into fiscal 2028 and in some cases, beyond, and the composition of our backlog remains healthy and well balanced. Equally as important is the mix of projects by size, complementing our mega projects that provide an anchor from a scheduling and execution perspective, we continue to see a steady flow of core projects below $10 million and larger projects in the $10 million to $50 million range. That blend of project scope and size lets us efficiently schedule around the natural stop and hold points that often arise in larger projects and enables us to optimize the variable costs of production.

Reflecting on fiscal 2026 results, I am particularly pleased with the continued progress we are making in our efforts to diversify Powell across the markets we serve. Traditionally, Powell has focused on delivering complex engineered-to-order electrical distribution solutions for customers spanning our important core industrial markets. Today, we are not only effectively serving these traditional Powell markets, but we are also successfully leveraging these same engineering and manufacturing competencies to continue to grow our presence across the electric utility and the commercial and other industrial end markets globally.

The current commercial demand spanning these end markets today demands process and structure that is embedded across our footprint, and it is a testament to our teams globally in their ability to scale and leverage the processes, engineering talent and manufacturing capabilities across the business. We are confident that this Powell attribute is a fundamental reason driving our success and an important competitive advantage for our business. Specific to our core industrial end markets, commercial activity remains strong. We continue to expand our position across the natural gas value chain, particularly in LNG as demonstrated by roughly $350 million of new LNG orders in the fiscal fourth quarter.

We were also encouraged by the fertilizer project awarded earlier in the year, which we believe is an early sign of a potential recovery in the petrochemical market following a period of softer market demand. Overall, the progress we have made against our decade-long strategy to diversify the business is increasingly evident in our results. The electric utility and commercial and other industrial markets represented 50% of revenue in fiscal 2026 compared to 41% in fiscal 2025. For perspective, these markets accounted for less than 30% of revenue on a significantly lower revenue base just 5 years ago.

We believe that this diversification is contributing to a more balanced business, reducing cyclicality and providing greater visibility to plan and invest beyond the current market cycles. Over the past year, we have taken a series of deliberate steps to add capacity. And together, they have expanded our manufacturing, office and warehouse footprint by more than 20% versus the end of fiscal 2025. In Ohio, we've added an incremental 60,000 square feet of manufacturing and warehousing capacity through a lease signed late last calendar year as we begin to execute on growing demand for our data center backlog. In Houston, we recently leased an additional 50,000 square feet of manufacturing and integration capacity.

While also establishing 2 satellite engineering offices in Southwest and Northwest Houston to deepen our engineering and design bench and broaden our coverage of the metro Houston area. Most significantly, we have substantially completed the Jacintoport expansion, adding 335,000 square feet of capacity, which is now operational. Additionally, we recently decided to further expand this location by an additional 80,000 square feet. This will be a world-class fabrication yard spanning roughly 1 million square feet with 1,200 feet of bulkhead for water access, ideal for shipping large single-piece power control rooms and large offshore modules.

With this expansion, we plan to support the accelerating demand for custom power control rooms targeted at core industrial applications, but this capacity will remain fungible across all the markets that we serve. At full utilization, we expect it to support well over $100 million of incremental annualized revenue. We are also looking forward and initiating the next phase of our capacity expansion strategy. During our fiscal third quarter of 2026, the Board authorized the lease of a new facility that will add approximately 275,000 square feet of manufacturing and integration space, which we expect to bring online in our fiscal third quarter of 2027.

Finally, we continue to evaluate a purpose-built greenfield Powell-owned factory of somewhere between 250,000 to 300,000 square feet, which would further support increased future fabrication needs for the markets that we serve. Now turning to the current operations. Labor availability and supply chain constraints remain 2 areas that we are closely monitoring. We are beginning to see increased competition for skilled craft labor across a broad geographic footprint. While this has not had an impact on our ability to execute our backlog to date, we remain mindful of the potential risk due to the increased demand for skilled labor as we look ahead to fiscal 2027 and 2028.

On the supply chain front, our teams continue to work closely with our key suppliers and partners to ensure material availability and delivery schedules remain aligned with our project commitments. As we enter fiscal 2027, the environment across each of our key verticals remains very active. We see continued momentum across most of the markets that we serve as evidenced by the fiscal 2026 order strength across our oil and gas, electric utility and commercial and other industrial market sectors. In our oil and gas sector, the most active end market is clearly being driven by the demand for LNG.

And we believe we are in the early innings of a multiyear infrastructure build-out and anticipate that this market domestically will remain active into the foreseeable future. Turning to our Electric Utility segment. The outlook remains robust and balanced across the customers and geographies that we serve. Demand continues to be underwritten by structurally undersupplied power generation and grid capacity and the growing wave of investment in electrical infrastructure is broad and durable. And finally, with respect to the data center opportunities that we are seeing, these are much more standard electrical applications versus our traditional engineered-to-order configurations, and we continue to find strong partners commercially that enable Powell to further penetrate this market.

On the electrical automation front, we are 1 year on from closing the Remsdaq acquisition, and it has proven synergistic and accretive across the company. The domestic data center market has pulled Remsdaq technology into the U.S. faster than we had planned, and it complements our medium voltage offerings on many of the data center orders that we secured throughout fiscal 2026. Additionally, we see a unique and valuable opportunity in U.S. government and defense, leveraging our U.S.-centric supply chain, operations and workforce, which position us well to support national defense or other governmental institutions for critical electrical distribution applications.

And finally, on M&A, our pipeline is healthy, and we are focused on complementary electrical products and/or markets expanding our breadth in automation and on building our services franchise. Valuations across the space are rich, so we will stay disciplined and act where we see both strategic fit and value. With that, I'd like to turn the call over to Mike to walk us through our financial results in greater detail.

Michael Metcalf: Thank you, Brett, and good morning, everyone. I will begin first with the fiscal fourth quarter business results and then move to the total fiscal year 2026 results. Revenues for the fourth fiscal quarter of 2026 increased by 33% to $397 million compared to the same quarter in fiscal 2025 of $298 million. This was also higher sequentially by $85 million, driven by strong output across our commercial and other industrial sector and to a lesser extent, a nice uptick across both the oil and gas as well as the utility sectors.

Net new orders for the fourth fiscal quarter were $710 million, $439 million higher than the same period 1 year ago, driven by strong year-over-year activity in our oil and gas and commercial and other industrial market sectors. During the quarter, we booked approximately $350 million of new orders, which consisted of 1 mega order of about $250 million as well as 1 mega data center order for roughly $85 million. Overall, we remain encouraged by the level of commercial activity across all of the end markets that we participate in.

Considering this level of new order bookings, coupled with the sustained strength of our top line performance, the book-to-bill ratio was 1.8x for the fiscal fourth quarter and 2.0x for the full year fiscal 2026. Reported backlog at the end of fiscal 2026 increased to $2.7 billion, $1.3 billion higher than the end of fiscal 2025 on strength across most of our key market sectors. Our core industrial end markets, oil and gas and petrochemical were 83% higher than the prior year period, while the electric utility sector increased by 34% and the commercial and other industrial sector grew by over 350% versus the prior year.

As we exit fiscal 2026, our backlog is very well balanced with 38% of the backlog consisting of our oil and gas and petrochemical sectors, while electric utility makes up 23% and 35% for commercial and other industrial, which is made up largely of data center orders. Overall, we are very pleased with both the execution across the business, driving record revenue levels for the year as well as our orders performance throughout fiscal 2026. Compared to the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, domestic revenues of $348 million increased by $118 million or 51%, while international revenues decreased by 29% to $48 million, driven primarily by the softer Canadian end market.

From a market sector perspective, revenues from our oil and gas and utility sectors were higher by 24% and 22%, respectively, on the solid commercial environment in the U.S., driving demand for the industrial build-out across both electrical infrastructure as well as LNG export terminals along the Gulf Coast. Additionally, our commercial and other industrial sector was higher by 179%, driven predominantly by the ongoing strength across the data center end market. Modestly offsetting this growth, our petrochemical and traction sectors were lower versus the same period 1 year ago by 49% and 24%, respectively.

We reported $138 million of gross profit in the fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, which was $45 million or 48% higher than the same period in fiscal 2025. Gross profit as a percentage of revenues increased by roughly 350 basis points to 34.9% of revenues in the current fiscal quarter. The higher quarterly margin rate is primarily attributable to strong project execution across the business, delivering favorable project closeouts, resulting in an incremental 230 basis points to the fourth fiscal quarter margin rate.

Additionally, we have maintained our pricing levels at or above the inflationary benchmarks across core commodities and engineered components that we consume in production, and when combined with the strong throughput and operational leverage that we are realizing across most of the Powell business units, these variables continue to generate a favorable tailwind to margins across most of our operating divisions. Selling, general and administrative expenses increased by $6.8 million or 25% on higher levels of compensation expenses as well as nonrecurring legal and professional expenses accrued in the period. SG&A expenses were $33.9 million in the fiscal fourth quarter or 8.5% of revenue compared to 9.1% of revenues in the same period a year ago.

In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, we reported net income of $81.5 million, generating $2.23 per diluted share compared to net income of $51.4 million or $1.41 per diluted share in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025. We generated $239 million of operating cash flow in the fiscal fourth quarter, driven mainly on the higher earnings and favorable contract milestones associated with the strong orders cadence during the period. Investments in property, plant and equipment totaled $8 million during the fiscal fourth quarter as we continue to focus on capacity and productivity projects across the business. Now recapping our total year fiscal 2026. Revenues of $1.3 billion increased by $152 million or 14% compared to fiscal 2025.

Most notably, our electric utility and commercial and other industrial sectors were higher versus fiscal 2025 by 21% and 65%, respectively, with the oil and gas sector also growing versus the prior fiscal year by 10%. The petrochemical and light rail traction sectors were lower versus the prior year by 42% and 11%, respectively. New orders booked in fiscal 2026 were $2.6 billion, 124% or $1.4 billion higher versus fiscal 2025. With the exception of the light rail traction sector, which was lower versus the prior year by 73%.

All of our end markets demonstrated strong year-over-year growth rates with the oil and gas and petrochemical booking activity higher by 108% and 134%, respectively, while the utility and commercial and other industrial market sectors grew 13% and 476%, respectively. Overall, throughout fiscal 2026, the business successfully leveraged the strong commercial environment that we've experienced across most of the end markets that we serve, resulting in a healthy mix of orders and backlog exiting fiscal 2026. Gross profit as a percentage of revenues grew 190 basis points year-over-year to 31.3% or $69 million higher than fiscal 2025.

The margin rate continues to benefit from a stable pricing environment, offsetting the current macro inflationary pressures while also leveraging Powell's global manufacturing footprint to maximize volume leverage and operational execution. Selling, general and administrative expenses were higher by $16 million versus the prior year. Overall, net SG&A expenses as a percentage of revenues were higher versus the prior year by 25 basis points at 8.9% of revenues in fiscal 2026 versus 8.6% in the prior year. We reported net income of $221.1 million or $6.04 per diluted share in fiscal 2026 compared to $180.7 million or $4.95 per diluted share in the prior year.

Operating cash flow generated in fiscal 2026 was $434 million versus $168 million in the prior year, driven by the higher order intake as well as the income generated versus the prior year. Total capital spending on property, plant and equipment was $18.5 million in fiscal 2026, $5.4 million higher than the prior year, driven in large part to the upgrade of our offshore fabrication yard as well as procuring additional fabrication equipment to address the capacity needs across the business.

At the end of fiscal 2026, we held cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments of $861 million, $385 million higher than our fiscal 2025 year-end position, reflecting the strong orders cadence throughout fiscal 2026 as well as the earnings generated by the business. The company holds 0 debt. Finally, in November 2026, we entered into a commitment increase and reallocation agreement with Bank of America and Texas Capital. Combined, this amendment increased our facility capacity to $200 million from the previous ceiling of $150 million. As we utilize this facility solely for commercial letters of credit, we felt that this was a prudent action in order to ensure our continued commercial success across the markets that we serve.

Looking forward, our priorities are clear. We remain focused on executing our growing backlog while concurrently bringing additional capacity online to address the strong market demand. We are optimistic that the momentum we experienced across our oil and gas, utility and commercial and other industrial end markets in fiscal 2026 will continue into fiscal 2027. The composition of our backlog is well balanced across our key end markets, while the quality of the backlog remains high and provides visibility well into fiscal 2028. With a stable pricing environment, high utilization across our North American manufacturing footprint and additional capacity coming online in fiscal 2027, we believe these factors position Powell for another strong year in fiscal 2027.

At this point, we'll be happy to answer your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question for today will come from Manish Somaiya with Cantor.

Michael Metcalf: Manish, this is Mike. I'll take that one. The margin profile for that particular project is really not much different than the rest of our aggregated backlog. I think that would be a big help to all of us.

Brett Cope: Yes. Manish, good question. We have the same question here. Certainly, we see the macroeconomic and certainly not missing the elections and how that's created a narrative out there. So we have been out. I've been out personally the last couple of weeks out meeting clients. And in the next couple of years, it doesn't seem to be a thing. Now could it be in 5 or 6 years? Could there be something developed with the change in the future?

I think in terms of funded projects and things that are rolling, I feel pretty bullish with what's out there. We've got to find our way into that. It doesn't change the work ahead of Powell, but the potential is very strong, and we're pretty excited.

Brett Cope: First of all, I'll walk through all 3 verticals. I feel really strong about especially our position in the U.S. and Canada here. And we're making good progress in the U.K. and some other areas on the IEC side of the electric standard, but the U.S. and Canada, really good visibility and getting better. Just the overall electrical one line, the distribution strategy, it can move really quickly depending on what's available. If I go back a couple of years ago, transformers were a great example where everybody were stacking in large powers and then they moved to medium power just because of availability of factory capacity.

And so we've noted on the call last couple of quarters about as we built flow lines, which we continue today to do, to build configure-to-order type approach to the market, that is allowing us to I don't want to say get over our skis, but take a little bit more calculated decision, not risk because what we're -- as we're learning how the velocity of this market can flow through our factories, we're able to go back and work with our clients going, okay, we feel better about what you're asking us.

#3067. Uber Adds Zoox’s Robotaxis to Its App. Everything to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

You could be paired with the boxy self-driving vehicles when hailing a ride in Las Vegas.

Starting this week, customers booking an Uber ride in Las Vegas could be matched with a Zoox autonomous vehicle.

Zoox’s boxy, purpose-built vehicles have been operating for the general public in Sin City for a little over a year via the company’s own app. But this is the first time Zoox, which is owned by Amazon, is teaming up with a third-party platform like Uber. (You can still hail a ride in Vegas through the Zoox app; the company began charging passengers in August.)

Now, riders who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric or Wait & Save could be paired with a Zoox robotaxi, and they won’t have to pay extra. You can boost your chances of being matched with the AV by going to Ride Preferences in the Uber app’s settings. Then tap Autonomous vehicles, and hit the toggle next to Get more autonomous rides.

After you’ve been matched with a Zoox vehicle, you can choose to accept the autonomous ride or opt for a non-AV. Passengers can access 24/7 human support from both the Uber app and inside the Zoox vehicle.

Unlike other autonomous vehicles from companies like Waymo and Wayve, which retrofit cars from third-party manufacturers, Zoox’s purpose-built robotaxis don’t have a steering wheel, driver’s seat or pedals. Instead, there are two rows of seats facing each other, so you can chat more easily with your fellow passengers. The vehicles are bidirectional, making it a little easier to get out of a parking space, for instance. I’ve taken a few Zoox rides in Las Vegas and San Francisco, and despite the robotaxi’s unique design, the experience felt remarkably ordinary, with the vehicle seamlessly navigating through traffic.

Uber and Zoox announced their multiyear partnership in March. The companies also plan to hit the road together in Los Angeles in 2027, after Zoox launches there via its own app.

Teaming up with Uber could expose Zoox to more customers, since many people already have the ride-hailing app downloaded on their phones. A tourist hub like Las Vegas has become a hotspot for AV companies to test and launch their services, with many people willing to try something new as they get around the city.

“Zoox has built something truly unique, and by bringing its purpose-built robotaxis to Uber, we’re introducing an entirely new riding experience to more people in Las Vegas, with Los Angeles coming next,” Samarth Kejriwal, global head of autonomous mobility at Uber, said in a statement.

This comes after the dissolution of Uber’s exclusive partnership with Alphabet-owned Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, which Bloomberg reports will end starting early next year. Instead, Waymo reportedly plans to offer rides directly within its own app, as it does in several other locations. Meanwhile, Uber has partnered with dozens of other AV companies, including Aurora, Wayve, Avride, Nuro and May Mobility.

While Waymo is the leader in the self-driving space, Zoox has been ramping up its operations in recent months. Along with Las Vegas, riders can join a waitlist to ride in San Francisco, with plans to roll out its robotaxi service in Miami and Austin. Zoox is also testing its self-driving technology in Seattle, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Dallas, Phoenix, Houston, San Diego and Washington, DC.

#3066. Lost or stolen Windows laptop? IT can lock it down without wiping it now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The Intune-enabled feature will allow admins to remotely lock down any compromised Windows device.

Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

The new remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.

Once a device is reported missing or stolen, an admin can disable login access from anywhere without having to fully wipe the laptop or smartphone. Microsoft reports that the lockdown will persist across restarts, even if the device is disconnected from Wi-Fi networks, and can only be lifted by an admin. This means that thieves can’t use your passwords, PINs, or biometric data to circumvent the lock.

While the new feature allows IT admins to respond quickly when a laptop or phone is reported missing, there are still security gaps that other Windows controls must address. The new lock feature doesn’t erase your data or wipe your device if it can’t be recovered, nor does it isolate the missing device from corporate networks. Therefore, IT admins will still need to access those controls via the Intune and Microsoft Entra dashboards.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up

The remote lock feature also doesn’t change your Microsoft account credentials, so you can use your log-ins on other devices to recover your data, change passwords, and temporarily disable permissions. Finally, Remote lock doesn’t block the device from being booted in Safe Mode, from a USB, in Windows Recovery Mode, or if the storage drive is reimaged; Microsoft highly recommends keeping BitLocker enabled until the device can be wiped or recovered.

Setting up the remote lock is a straightforward process: Log into the Intune management center, then go to Devices > Windows > Configuration > Create > New Policy > Windows 10 and later > Templates > Custom. This lets admins create a profile for each network-connected device and a device group reserved for lockdown. Locking down a device is as simple as adding it to the group. To unlock, create a second profile and device group, and move the locked device to the new unlock category.
